Bhupen's hostel room in the Tezpur college was always noisy in the evenings, and his flashcards for the English entrance test sat in a rubber band on the shelf, untouched. Every night he promised himself he'd do them. Every night he didn't.
His senior Naveen said, "You brush your teeth every morning without fail, right?"
"Obviously."
"Then tie the cards to that. After brushing, five cards. Nothing else."
The next morning Bhupen brushed his teeth at the corridor sink, came back, and picked up five cards from the stack by his toothbrush mug. Five words. Two minutes.
By the end of the month, the rubber band had moved to a second stack: words he knew. He hadn't missed a single morning, because he hadn't missed a single brushing.

qa.q: How many cards did Bhupen do after brushing?
How had Bhupen been feeling about the untouched flashcards?
qa.a: He was probably guilty and frustrated, promising himself every night and never doing them.

qa.q: Why did linking the cards to brushing work better than promising to do them at night?
qa.a: Because brushing already happens every morning without fail, so it reminds him automatically, while the noisy evenings kept pushing the cards aside.

qa.q: How does Naveen's suggestion look to Bhupen at first?
qa.a: It seems almost too simple at first, but it gives Bhupen a small habit he actually keeps.

grounding: It shows a student attaching five flashcards to morning tooth-brushing, so the new habit hooks onto a routine that is already stable.

subtype: Approach: attaches a new habit to an existing cue [Action]

In the small flat in Taipei, Wei shared a bathroom with his sister Xin and was always rushing in the mornings. His language-exam flashcards lived in a drawer. He meant to study at night, but by night he was too tired.
Xin suggested something she'd read about. "Don't find new time. Hook it to something you already do."
"Like what?"
"You brush your teeth every day. After that, five cards."
So he put the flashcard box beside the sink. Every morning, toothbrush back in the cup, then five cards, reading each one aloud while the kettle boiled.
After three weeks, he'd gone through the whole box once. He told Xin, "I never had to remember. The toothbrush remembers for me."

qa.q: Where did Wei put the flashcard box?
qa.a: He put the flashcard box beside the sink.

qa.q: How might Wei have been feeling about his flashcards before the change?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and guilty, meaning to study at night but always too tired.

qa.q: What else could Wei hook to another daily routine?
qa.a: He could review five old cards while waiting for the bus, since that is another thing he does every day.

qa.q: How might Xin see Wei going through the whole box?
qa.a: Xin may feel pleased and a little proud that her suggestion worked for her brother.

grounding: It shows a student attaching flashcard revision to brushing his teeth each morning, so the habit hooks onto an existing routine.
